content: 1. Berry RJ and colleagues conducted a study in China demonstrating that folic acid supplementation effectively prevents neural tube defects. This was part of a collaborative project aimed at reducing the incidence of these congenital anomalies. (N Engl J Med, 1999; 341(20):1485–90). 2. Pfeiffer CM et al. highlighted the importance of assessing vitamin status in large population surveys by measuring biomarkers and dietary intake. They used folate and vitamin D as case studies to illustrate the methodology. (Food Nutr Res, 2012; 56:5944). 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed standards for maternal and neonatal care, emphasizing integrated management of pregnancy and childbirth to improve health outcomes. (Accessed February 6, 2015). 4. Berti C and colleagues performed a meta-analysis examining folate intake and biomarkers of folate status in women of reproductive age, pregnant women, and lactating women, providing critical insights into nutritional needs during these life stages. (J Nutr Metab, 2012; 2012:470656). 5. Botto LD and Yang Q reviewed the relationship between 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) gene variants and congenital anomalies, providing a comprehensive analysis of genetic influences on folate metabolism. (Am J Epidemiol, 2000; 151(9):862–77). 6. Shane B provided an overview of folate and vitamin B12 metabolism, discussing their interactions with riboflavin, vitamin B6, and genetic polymorphisms, which are critical for understanding metabolic pathways and their clinical implications. (Food Nutr Bull, 2008; 29(2 Suppl.):S5–16). 7. Crider KS et al. demonstrated that the MTHFR 677C→T genotype is associated with variations in folate and homocysteine concentrations in a large, population-based, double-blind trial of folic acid supplementation. (Am J Clin Nutr, 2011; 93(6):1365–72). 8. Wilcken B and colleagues investigated the geographical and ethnic variation of the 677C→T allele of the MTHFR gene, analyzing data from over 7,000 newborns across 16 regions worldwide. (J Med Genet, 2003; 40(8):619–25). 9. Tinker SC et al. explored whether obesity modifies the relationship between supplemental folic acid intake and folate status among nonpregnant women of childbearing age in the United States. (Birth Defects Res A Clin Mol Teratol, 2012; 94(10):749–55). 10. Nzila A et al. examined the impact of folate supplementation on the efficacy of sulfadoxine/pyrimethamine in preventing malaria during pregnancy, focusing on the potential role of 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate. (J Antimicrob Chemother, 2014; 69(2):323–30). 11. Gregson A and Plowe CV reviewed the mechanisms of resistance of malaria parasites to antifolates, providing insights into the challenges of treating malaria in the context of drug resistance. (Pharmacol Rev, 2005; 57(1):117–45). 12. The WHO guideline on optimal serum and red blood cell folate concentrations in women of reproductive age aims to prevent neural tube defects by establishing evidence-based thresholds for folate levels. (Accessed February 6, 2015). 13. Nutritional anaemias were addressed in a 1968 WHO report, which provided foundational knowledge on the causes, prevention, and treatment of anaemia, particularly iron deficiency. (WHO Technical Report Series, 1968). 14. de Benoist B summarized the conclusions of a WHO technical consultation on folate and vitamin B12 deficiencies, emphasizing the global health implications of these nutrient deficiencies. (Food Nutr Bull, 2008; 29(2 Suppl.):S238–44). 15. Baker H et al. developed a microbiological method for detecting folic acid deficiency in humans, which has been widely used in clinical and research settings. (Clin Chem, 1959; 5(4):275–80). 16. Pfeiffer CM et al. compared serum and red blood cell folate measurements using microbiological assays in national population surveys, highlighting the importance of assay standardization. (J Nutr, 2011; 141(7):1402–9). 17. Anderson BB and Cowan JD investigated the effect of light on the Lactobacillus casei microbiological assay, which is critical for accurate folate measurement. (Am J Clin Pathol, 1968; 21(1):85–7). 18. Yetley EA et al. summarized a roundtable discussion on biomarkers of folate status in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), emphasizing the need for robust biomarkers in public health monitoring. (Am J Clin Nutr, 2011; 94(1):303S–12S). 19. Fazili Z et al. compared serum folate species analyzed by LC-MS/MS with total folate measured by microbiological assay and Bio-Rad radioassay, demonstrating the strengths and limitations of each method. (Clin Chem, 2007; 53(4):781–4). 20. Higgins J and Green S edited the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, providing methodological guidance for conducting high-quality systematic reviews. (Updated March 2011). 21. Bailey L et al. reviewed biomarkers of nutrition for development (BOND) with a focus on folate, providing a comprehensive resource for understanding folate's role in health and disease. (Personal communication, 2015). 22. Tsang BL et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the association between the MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism and blood folate concentrations, integrating data from trials and observational studies. (Am J Clin Nutr, 2015). 23. Marchetta CM et al. systematically reviewed the relationship between natural food folate intake and blood folate concentrations, using Bayesian meta-analysis to synthesize evidence from trials and observational studies. (Nutrients, 2015; 7:2663–86). 24. Yan L et al. analyzed the association of the maternal MTHFR C677T polymorphism with susceptibility to neural tube defects in offspring, based on evidence from 25 case-control studies. (PLoS One, 2012; 7(10):e41689). 25. De-Regil LM et al. evaluated the effects and safety of periconceptional folate supplementation for preventing birth defects, providing evidence-based recommendations. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2010; CD007950). 26. Daly LE et al. demonstrated the relationship between folate levels and neural tube defects, emphasizing the implications for prevention strategies. (JAMA, 1995; 274(21):1698–702). 27. Crider KS et al. used Bayesian modeling to estimate population red blood cell folate concentrations required for neural tube defect prevention, providing a quantitative framework for public health interventions. (BMJ, 2014; 349:g4554). 28. Clarke R and Derrick B discussed the importance of tracking red blood cell folate concentrations to guide policy decisions on fortification for neural tube defect prevention. (BMJ, 2014; 349:g4810). 29. Shea BJ et al. validated the AMSTAR tool for assessing the methodological quality of systematic reviews, ensuring reliability in evidence synthesis. (J Clin Epidemiol, 2009; 62(10):1013–20). 30. Fernandez-Gaxiola AC and De-Regil LM reviewed the efficacy of intermittent iron supplementation in reducing anaemia and its associated impairments in menstruating women. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2011; CD009218). 31. Lassi ZS et al. evaluated the impact of folic acid supplementation during pregnancy on maternal health and pregnancy outcomes, providing evidence for clinical practice. (Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2013; CD006896). 32. Berry RJ et al. discussed the role of folic acid fortification in preventing neural tube defects, highlighting its public health significance. (In: Bailey L, ed. Folate in Health and Disease, 2010). 33. Pfeiffer CM et al. analyzed folate status in the U.S. population before and after fortification, using assay-adjusted data from NHANES 1988–2010. (J Nutr, 2012; 142(5):886–93). 34. Suchdev P et al. reviewed the use of multiple micronutrient powders for home fortification of foods in pregnant women, emphasizing their role in addressing micronutrient malnutrition. (WHO e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions, 2011). 35. Peña-Rosas J et al. explored the fortification of rice with vitamins and minerals as a strategy to combat micronutrient malnutrition, providing practical recommendations. (Personal communication, 2015). 36. Pfeiffer C et al. contributed a chapter on biochemical indices in the Encyclopedia of Human Nutrition, detailing methods for assessing nutritional status. (3rd ed., 2013). 37. The WHO Vitamin and Mineral Nutrition Information System provides guidelines for assessing folate status in populations, emphasizing the importance of serum and red blood cell folate concentrations. (Accessed February 6, 2015). 38. Molloy AM and Scott JM described a microbiological assay for measuring serum, plasma, and red cell folate, which is widely used in clinical and research settings. (Methods Enzymol, 1997; 281:43–53). 39. Marchetta CM and Hamner HC analyzed blood folate concentrations among women of childbearing age by race/ethnicity and acculturation, using NHANES data from 2001–2010. (Matern Child Nutr, 2014). 40. Fuller-Deets M and Dingwall R discussed the ethical implications of strategies to improve folate intake in women of reproductive age, addressing public health and policy considerations. (Accessed February 6, 2015).
